name: Town of Groton

actions.title: One-Year Moratorium on Large Data Centers (>5,000 sq ft)
actions.summary: Groton's Planning and Zoning Commission approved a one-year ban on applications for data centers larger than 5,000 square feet to allow time to develop permanent regulations.

actions.title: Permanent Zoning Regulation Capping Data Centers at 12,500 sq ft
actions.summary: Following its moratorium, Groton unanimously adopted permanent zoning rules banning data centers larger than 12,500 square feet and restricting them to light-industrial zones, converting the moratorium into a lasting size cap.

actions.title: Rejection of NE Edge Large-Scale Data Center Proposals
actions.summary: Groton officials ceased discussions with NE Edge after the company proposed two 250,000 sq ft data centers near the Millstone nuclear power station, citing concerns about community impact and infrastructure.

contextBlurb: Groton is Connecticut's most active municipal regulator of data centers, having used a 2022 one-year moratorium as a bridge to adopt permanent zoning rules in July 2023 that cap facility size at 12,500 square feet and limit siting to light-industrial zones. The town's action was driven by failed proposals from GotSpace Data Partners and NE Edge to build hyperscale facilities near the Millstone nuclear power station. Groton's approach—moratorium followed by permanent zoning—has since been cited as a model by Morris, West Haven, and New Haven.

name: Town of Morris

actions.title: Two-Year Data Center Development Moratorium
actions.summary: Morris's Planning and Zoning Commission approved a two-year moratorium on data center development to protect farmland and rural character while the town drafts permanent land-use regulations.

contextBlurb: Morris, a small rural town in Litchfield County, enacted a two-year data center moratorium in May 2026 primarily to protect its farmland and rural character, citing that data centers typically require large land footprints that often consume agricultural land. No formal data center proposal had yet been filed in Morris; officials acted proactively, concerned that state-level siting authority through the Connecticut Siting Council could override local zoning. The town is using the moratorium period to evaluate environmental, infrastructure, and public-safety impacts and align future rules with its Plan of Conservation and Development.

name: City of West Haven

actions.title: 12-Month Moratorium on Data Center Establishment and Development
actions.summary: West Haven's City Council unanimously enacted a 12-month moratorium suspending permit processing and zoning actions for data centers to allow planners time to study electrical demand, cooling, siting, and other impacts.

contextBlurb: West Haven's City Council voted unanimously on June 8, 2026, to impose a 12-month moratorium on data center development, with Mayor Durinda Borer citing the absence of city zoning or licensing rules specific to large-scale data facilities. The pause covers all new data center permits and zoning approvals while municipal planners study electrical demand, cooling system impacts, and appropriate siting standards. West Haven is one of several Connecticut municipalities—alongside Groton and Morris—cited by New Haven as precedents for its own proposed moratorium.

name: City of New Haven

actions.title: Proposed 12-Month Data Center Development Moratorium Ordinance
actions.summary: Board of Alders Majority Leader Richard Furlow introduced a proposed ordinance imposing a 12-month ban on new data center permits and conversions to give the city time to craft zoning regulations, with City Plan Commission review scheduled for July 15, 2026.

contextBlurb: New Haven lacks any zoning regulations specific to data centers, prompting Alderman Richard Furlow to introduce a proposed 12-month moratorium ordinance in July 2026 in response to constituent concerns—even though no data center application is currently pending. The ordinance would direct the city's economic development department to convene a working group with six months to recommend zoning standards. New Haven explicitly cited precedents set by Groton, Morris, and West Haven in the text of its proposed ordinance amendment.
